policy_title: Create a Border Security Command and Reform the Asylum System
stated: Labour will create a new Border Security Command with hundreds of investigators and cross-border police officers, funded by ending the Rwanda scheme, to dismantle criminal gangs behind small boat crossings. They will seek a new security agreement with the EU for intelligence sharing. The party will also clear the asylum backlog by hiring additional caseworkers to end the use of asylum hotels, set up a new returns and enforcement unit with 1,000 staff to fast-track removals to safe countries, and work with international partners to address humanitarian crises causing displacement.

source.quote: Labour will stop the chaos and go after the criminal gangs who trade in driving this crisis. We will create a new Border Security Command, with hundreds of new investigators, intelligence officers, and cross-border police officers. This will be funded by ending the wasteful Migration and Economic Development partnership with Rwanda. This new Command will work internationally and be supported by new counter-terrorism style powers, to pursue, disrupt, and arrest those responsible for the vile trade. We will seek a new security agreement with the EU to ensure access to real-time intelligence and enable our policing teams to lead joint investigations with their European counterparts. Labour will turn the page and restore order to the asylum system so that it operates swiftly, firmly, and fairly; and the rules are properly enforced. We will hire additional caseworkers to clear the Conservatives’ backlog and end asylum hotels, saving the taxpayer billions of pounds. Labour will set up a new returns and enforcement unit, with an additional 1,000 staff, to fast-track removals to safe countries for people who do not have the right to stay here. We will negotiate additional returns arrangements to speed up returns and increase the number of safe countries that failed asylum seekers can swiftly be sent back to. And we will also act upstream, working with international partners to address the humanitarian crises which lead people to flee their homes, and to strengthen support for refugees in their home region.

bearing_set.reason: Directly targets criminal gangs running people-smuggling operations, border security infrastructure, and enforcement/removal units — core safety & security and justice-system measures.

Ending use of costly asylum hotels and reducing asylum backlog has a plausible non-negligible effect on public expenditure and associated fiscal pressures that feed into household costs and public service funding.

Fast-track removals and expedited asylum processing bear directly on due process and rule of law for asylum claimants — the concrete mechanism is that accelerated procedures may limit access to legal challenge and representation, a specific indicator of the due-process strand of O9.

Significant and contested fiscal effects on both sides: stated savings from ending the Rwanda scheme vs. new staffing costs (caseworkers + 1,000 enforcement staff), offset by potentially large savings from ending asylum hotels (Home Office figures put hotel costs at ~£8m/day at peak); the net funded-vs-borrowed picture is non-negligible.

membership_note: Three clear bearings: a direct national-security/crime effect (O5), a due-process/rule-of-law effect on asylum seekers (O9), and material but contested fiscal consequences (O12). Effects on cohesion (O15), prosperity (O13), or other fundamentals are too indirect and speculative to clear the non-negligible bar at this stage.
